speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I thought that it might be more convenient for Members to have copies so that they can refer to them as I am speaking.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the Motions are of a far deeper and greater significance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fundamentally, the Motions are about safeguarding the essence of democracy – our democracy – and preserving its most vital and essential characteristic, which is, trust.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are about the need to ensure the integrity of our institutions, and Parliament in particular, and about the confidence Singaporeans can have in their elected representatives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Established democracies, like Australia and the United Kingdom, have, in recent months, had to deal with allegations of senior parliamentarians being untruthful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The consequences are the erosion of public trust.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Now, regrettably, we have to deal with our own situation of parliamentarians being untruthful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How we deal with this will reflect on our values and the standards of conduct to which we hold ourselves as MPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On 3 August 2021, Ms Khan spoke during the debate on the Workers' Party's Motion titled "Empowering Women".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She claimed that the Police's response to sexual assault survivors who lodged Police reports was sometimes "disheartening".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She alleged that three years ago, she had accompanied a sexual assault survivor to make a Police report against a rape that was committed against the survivor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She claimed to have witnessed the survivor come out crying.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police officer had allegedly made comments about her dressing and the fact that she had been drinking.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee was duly convened and began its inquiry on 29 November 2021.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, in the course of its inquiry, the conduct of three senior members of the Workers' Party leadership also came into question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This led the Committee to also make certain findings and recommendations relating to them as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Before I go into the Report, Mr Speaker, let me say something about the privileges and immunities of Parliament and the corresponding duty that arises.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the most powerful things about a parliamentary democracy is the ability to speak freely and candidly in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is so that MPs can raise matters of public importance, safe in the knowledge that they have immunity from civil or criminal proceedings outside this House.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Singapore, this is enshrined in the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act 1962, the PPIPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But because it is such an important privilege, it must also be used responsibly and must not be abused.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This includes the need to be truthful on, and to be able to substantiate, matters said in Parliament or any committee of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other aspect of parliamentary democracy is that MPs are expected to act honourably and to respect the processes of Parliament as an institution, and not act in a manner that would undermine it or the work of its committees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Thus, dishonourable conduct, abuse of privilege and contempt of Parliament, including its committees, are offences under the PPIPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parliament is expected to keep its own House in order.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, the Act gives Parliament power to deal with such offences ranging from a reprimand, suspension of privileges from Parliament, a fine or even committal to prison and expulsion from Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, if the conduct constitutes an offence listed under Part 5 of the PPIPA, Parliament also has the power to refer the matter to the Public Prosecutor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, in respect of Ms Raeesah Khan for abuse of privilege.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of liability, the case against Ms Khan is clear and straightforward.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She has admitted that she lied in Parliament twice on 3 August 2021 and again on 4 October.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee has, therefore, found she “acted with disregard for the dignity and decorum of the House” and recommended that Parliament find Ms Khan guilty of abuse of privilege on all three occasions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You will see that this is dealt with in para 2(a) of the First Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The next issue is what penalty she should receive for these abuses of privilege.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Here, it is undisputed that when she lied on 3 August, she was the only one who knew that what she had said was untrue and, therefore, acted entirely of her own accord.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, she should bear the full and sole responsibility for those transgressions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is dealt with in para 2(b) of the First Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I turn now to the penalty for the lie that was repeated on 4 October 2021.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the issue that occupied the bulk of the Committee’s inquiry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because by this time, she had disclosed the Untruth to the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, and the two senior Workers’ Party (WP) leaders, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap, who are the Chairman and the Vice Chairman of WP respectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the issue is this: when Ms Khan repeated the lie in Parliament on 4 October, was she acting on her own accord or was she acting on the guidance of her senior party leaders?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If she was acting on her own, then the penalty should be higher, because it means that she and she alone was responsible for deliberately repeating the lie despite being told otherwise – as claimed by Mr Pritam Singh – showing a lack of remorse.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if as a young and inexperienced MP, she was acting on the instructions or guidance of her party leaders, to whom she deferred and to whose views she gave weight, then that would be a mitigating factor, because then she is not the only one responsible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, the penalty should be lower.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Here, the accounts of Ms Raeesah Khan and the three senior WP leaders are diametrically opposed – so much so that, in fact, there can be no possibility of this being a case of differing interpretations or of any misunderstanding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a situation where either Ms Raeesah Khan lied to the Committee, or else Mr Pritam Singh, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap lied to the Committee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Khan’s evidence is that when she repeated the lie on 4 October, it was her understanding, based on what Mr Singh said to her on 3 October, that there would be no consequences if she continued with the Untruth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh, on the other hand, says that Ms Khan did so on her own accord and contrary to instructions given.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Lim and Mr Faisal say they did not discuss the issue with her.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Two meetings are key to this issue: the meeting between Ms Khan and the three senior WP leaders on 8 August 2021, or "the 8 August meeting”, and the meeting between Mr Singh and Ms Khan on 3 October 2021 at her home, or “the 3 October meeting”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Regarding the 8 August meeting, Ms Khan’s evidence was that the three senior WP leaders told her to continue with the Untruth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was no need for her to clarify the truth in Parliament, and Mr Singh told her to “take the information to the grave”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The three WP leaders, on the other hand, say that there was simply no discussion on the matter after Ms Khan confessed to them, or, indeed, for nearly two months which passed thereafter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Instead, the discussion moved on to other matters.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is of critical importance because it took place the evening before the Parliament Sitting of 4 October, where Ms Khan said the lie for the third time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This meeting involved just Ms Khan and Mr Singh.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The issue with regard to the 3 October meeting was whether Mr Singh had made it clear to Ms Khan that she had to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Or Mr Singh gave Ms Khan a choice as to whether to tell the truth or keep to the Untruth, and if he did give her such a choice, whether he pointed her in the direction of how that choice should be exercised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Khan’s evidence is that “the conversation was that if   were to retain the narrative or if   were to continue the narrative, there would be no judgement”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Her understanding of this therefore was that there would be no consequences if she continued with the lie.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She was not instructed to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh’s evidence, on the other hand, was that he did not give Ms Khan a choice and that he made it “crystal clear” that she had to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Presented with such conflicting evidence, there is only one way to tell who is telling the truth, and, that is, to test it against objective evidence, which is what the Committee did.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They assessed it against the contemporaneous evidence, against written documents, against the conduct of the parties both before and after the relevant events, and they tested it against whether the evidence given to the Committee made sense.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there is written, contemporaneous evidence immediately after the meeting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (b) Her evidence was corroborated by Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (c) On the three WP leaders’ own evidence, between 8 August and 3 October, nothing was discussed about clarifying the lie, but they all agreed that telling the Untruth in Parliament was a serious matter and should be corrected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (d) There were no correspondence or documents from them on the issue at all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (e) They did not speak with Ms Khan on the issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (f) While Mr Singh had claimed he was concerned with ensuring that Ms Khan’s family was told about the sexual assault before clarifying the Untruth, not once did he or the others check if she had spoken with her parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (g) No steps were taken for any clarification to be made in Parliament, ahead of the September or October Sittings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (h) The other WP CEC members were kept in the dark.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh established a Disciplinary Panel consisting of the very same people who knew that she lied – himself, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap – and they did not disclose this to the CEC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All of these are consistent with a situation in which she was told to maintain the lie.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He did not tell Ms Lim or Mr Faisal Manap about the meeting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (b) At this meeting, Mr Singh did not tell Ms Khan to proactively raise the matter, or to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not disputed but this common position was only arrived at after inconsistencies in Mr Singh’s evidence was pointed out and he changed his evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (c) Mr Singh initially said Ms Khan had to proactively clarify the truth on 4 October even if the issue did not come up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But when it was pointed out that no preparations had been made, there were no draft statements, for example, then he said no preparatory steps were taken because it was uncertain if Ms Khan would have to clarify the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At this point, he realised his earlier evidence was untenable and he changed his position and admitted that he did not tell Ms Khan to come clean proactively on 4 October.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He then said she should tell the truth if raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (d) But Mr Singh’s claim that he made clear on 3 October that Ms Khan should clarify the truth if raised is contradicted by the fact that no preparation whatsoever was made prior to 4 October to prepare for the truth to be told.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Lim admitted, in the context of whether it would have been possible on 4 October to have Ms Lim clarify the truth the next day on 5 October, that this was not possible because time was needed to carefully structure Ms Khan’s clarification and to make the necessary preparations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is borne out by what happened after the decision was taken to come clean on 12 October when the whole WP machinery swung into action – there were discussions on what the draft statement should look like, the drafts were personally vetted by Mr Singh and shown to their CEC, their activists and their social media teams were prepped and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (e) On 4 October, as Minister Shanmugam was asking Ms Khan in this Chamber to confirm if the incident had really occurred as she had described, Ms Khan texted Mr Pritam Singh to ask “What shall I do Pritam?” If, as he claimed, he had been clear that, if asked, she should tell the truth, there would have been no need for her to text him for guidance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (f) Further, if Mr Singh’s evidence was true, it would mean that when Ms Khan lied again on 4 October, she would have flagrantly disobeyed his instruction of the previous day.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you would expect that in such a situation, he would immediately have demanded an explanation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Yet Mr Singh did not speak to Ms Khan for the rest of the day, until close to midnight.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And even then, there was no instruction to clarify the truth the following day on 5 October when Parliament was still sitting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (g) Mr Singh told Ms Khan that he would not “judge her”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This makes no sense if he had told Ms Khan to tell the truth, as there would be nothing to judge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, it makes a lot of sense if he had told or encouraged her to continue the lie.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (h) Ms Loh Pei Ying’s and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan’s evidence contradict what Mr Singh said.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On 12 October, Mr Singh told Ms Loh and Mr Nathan that he had met Ms Khan on 3 October and told her “I will not judge you”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Both Ms Low and Mr Nathan understood this to mean that Mr Singh had given Ms Khan a choice as to whether or not to come clean, and that if she chose to repeat the Untruth she would not be judged.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (i) Mr Singh claimed he did not give Ms Khan a choice as to whether to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this is contradicted by Ms Lim’s notes taken during the Disciplinary Panel, in which she recorded Mr Singh as telling Ms Khan that “I told you it was your call”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (j) On 7 October, Ms Khan had sent an email to Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap seeking their advice on what to do because she had just received an email from the Police requesting her assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In her email, she thanked the senior WP leaders “for listening to me, for caring for me and for guiding me throughout this without judgement”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee found that if Mr Singh had, indeed, told Ms Khan on 3 October to tell the truth, then after she lied again on 4 October, which would have been a breach of that instruction, she would not be thanking them for guiding her without judgement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Implicit in her email is that she had followed their guidance until then.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee found that by telling Ms Khan on 3 October that "there would be no judgement", Mr Singh had left her with the view that if she were to continue with the Untruth, there would be no judgement on her.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee further found that taken together, the events of the 8 August and 3 October meetings would essentially point Ms Khan in one direction, which is, to keep to the Untruth if the issue was raised, with the assurance that Mr Singh would not judge her if she did so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee considered that Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap's conduct could constitute contempt of Parliament and offences under Part 5 of the PPIPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the Committee was convened to look into the complaint against Ms Khan, the Committee noted that it was beyond its purview to recommend any penalty in respect of the three senior Workers' Party leaders for their conduct which arose in the course of the inquiry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parliament, however, has the power to consider what should be done and take the appropriate action.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To assist Parliament in this task, the Committee has made the following recommendations for our consideration: (a)	that while Parliament has the option to refer the three senior Workers' Party leaders to another Committee of Privileges, it is unlikely that another Committee would make much progress in terms of uncovering more evidence; and (b)	that a distinction should be drawn between the conduct of Mr Singh on the one hand, and Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap on the other, given their different roles and conduct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee noted Ms Lim's and Mr Faisal Manap's roles were "relatively subsidiary", while Mr Singh appeared to have played "the key and leading role in guiding Ms Khan in respect of the Untruth".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is addressed in paragraph 2 of the Second Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Others may also wonder why it is the case that, for Ms Khan, who lied to Parliament, a fine is proposed whereas in the case of Mr Singh, who also lied, but to a Committee of Parliament, he should be referred to the Public Prosecutor (PP) instead of just being fined like Ms Khan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are important questions and I want to address them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the PPIPA, there are what, I would term, and this is my term, general offences: offences of dishonourable conduct, abuse of privilege and contempt.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These, Parliament can and often would deal with itself.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But there is also a certain category of offences which could be dishonourable conduct or you could classify them as contempt, but they are very specific under Part 5 of the PPIPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include lying to a Committee in Parliament and refusing to answer questions as well as refusing to produce documents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are other offences listed in Part 5.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What is common about them and why they are also regarded as serious, is that they, essentially, pervert, obstruct or prevent the processes of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the Part 5 offences, Parliament has the power to refer these to the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The PPIPA does not provide for other offences to be referred to the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you could have an offence, which is a Part 5 offence, but which Parliament may choose not to refer, if it does not think it is that serious.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this case, the Committee found that all three lied, but it is only recommending to refer Mr Singh to the PP, not Ms Sylvia Lim, not Mr Faisal Manap because their roles were subsidiary and their lies were not as egregious.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then you may ask, so what is the difference between Mr Pritam Singh's lie and Ms Khan's?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The seriousness of the conduct on the part of Mr Singh is this: (a) Ms Khan lied to Parliament, and that was bad enough.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But Mr Singh on the other hand, if what the Committee found is correct, not only lied but lied under oath.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And not only that, but this was in proceedings before a Select Committee of Parliament conducting a formal inquiry and tasked with finding out the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, there is the question of the consequences of a lie in this context – because it would, if believed, have had a bearing on the punishment to be meted out to Ms Khan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The lies would have determined the fate of another MP who was being looked at before the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is a different order of seriousness altogether.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is a Part 5 offence under the PPIPA, and that is the reason why the Committee had recommended referring Mr Singh to the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (b) The other thing is that it would mean Ms Khan was following his guidance when she lied on 4 October.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (c) So, given the seriousness of the matter, it would be the fairest course of action to all concerned to refer it to the PP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The PP will have the opportunity to consider all evidence afresh, including new evidence, in deciding whether or not to prefer criminal charges against Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would also give Mr Singh the opportunity to defend and vindicate himself, with legal counsel, if criminal charges are brought.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (d) Fourth, the matter would be adjudicated by the Courts which are independent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is addressed in paragraph 2 of the Second Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is dealt with in para 3(i) of the Second Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is dealt with in paragraphs 3(i) to (ii) of the Second Motion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parliament will only consider the remaining issues (if any) after the criminal justice process has taken its course, by which time we will have the benefit of what emerges from that process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the fairest way forward for all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would ask Members to accept them and to support the Motions, as I do, so as to uphold public trust in Parliament and in our democracy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In accordance with the earlier decision of this House to have a simultaneous debate on both Motions, I will now call on Members to make their speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are allowed to consider both Motions in a single speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any Member who wishes to vote against either Motion can do so directly without such amendments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It has been about 25 years since a Committee of Privileges (COP) Report has been tabled in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When seen as a whole, the COP's processes and the Report before Parliament leave many questions, gaps and omissions and, by extension, suggest political partisanship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A key question is: who did this House commit to the COP?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The COP did not appear to want to get to the bottom of why Ms Khan lied in Parliament nor why she had a propensity to lie with respect to her anecdote, both in and out of this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact that she had concocted a lie to bolster her anecdote in Parliament was not balanced against her evidence to the COP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What took centre stage instead was her uncorroborated testimony that she was instructed to take her lie to the grave by the Workers' Party leadership, a fabrication which never came out from any witness at the COP except Ms Raeesah Khan herself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on two main areas before concluding with a section on candidate selection in the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will reflect on my judgement with respect to Ms Khan's reasons for lying in Parliament, arising from my meeting with her on 8 August.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will raise some broad points about the selective nature of how the COP Report dealt with the evidence before it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, as I intend to clear my name and cooperate with the Public Prosecutor, my comments on the COP Report will be limited in scope.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The most difficult aspect of this episode for me personally, and most certainly something that I have reflected on, is the approach to take when a fellow MP tells you, first, she is a rape victim; and second, how this episode caused an untruth to be told in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the moment I learned after the August Sitting that Ms Khan had lied in Parliament, there was no doubt in my mind that she would have to confess in Parliament that she had lied and that she would have to apologise for it in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have shared publicly that the matter of the lie was something for Ms Khan to explain in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My firm belief is that a Member of Parliament must be accountable in Parliament for what they say in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I considered that whenever she confessed, Ms Khan would have to explain her reason for telling her lie.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not want Ms Khan's parents or loved ones to be caught by surprise before she had a chance to speak with them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Looking back though, I gave Ms Khan too much time to settle herself before closing this issue with her.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Between 8 August and 30 September, I should have been proactive and checked where she was in addressing the matter with her family.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledged the same to the COP in my evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I will continue to be as sympathetic to anyone who shares such deeply personal details with me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My instinct, even today, would be to keep the information of the sexual assault to myself, or to a very small group of trusted individuals, given its highly personal and sensitive nature.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would allow such a person space to deal with the matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I still believe that it was right that the clarification was made in Parliament rather than out of it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That said, I will discuss with my party colleagues how, as an organisation and political party, we can handle such matters better while taking into account how delicate they are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For today, the principal point I will make is the disregard of evidence I submitted to the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At minimum, I would have expected a listing of all the documents my fellow Workers' Party colleagues and I submitted to the Committee to be included in the COP Report, to indicate that they were actively considered in deliberations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I can only assume they were not considered, despite my colleagues and I being served with a summons to produce.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are objective documents that I submitted to the Committee which raised serious doubts about the eventual findings reached in the Report, including the unparliamentary language used at various places, which is not supported by evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The following points need to be considered as to why I mentioned the psychiatric evaluation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the notes of the Workers' Party Disciplinary Panel, or DP, which was submitted to the COP show that Ms Khan tendered on her own accord, documents which revealed that she was the patient of a psychotherapist who had referred her to a psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, on 29 November, Ms Khan voluntarily shared with the DP that she suffered from dissociation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once again, the relevant DP notes were forwarded to the COP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And third, I was asked an open question by the COP as to why Ms Khan would make certain statements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I attempted to give a fair answer in line with what Ms Khan herself had revealed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the COP was indeed a fact-finding body, should I not have raised the matter of Ms Khan possibly labouring under a condition to the COP?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my evidence to the COP, I registered the point that the matter was raised because it covered issues of proportionality and culpability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I reject this assertion that in raising the matter of Ms Khan's mental health to a fact-finding body with a view to consider an appropriate punishment, I had somehow smeared her, or worse, somehow cast aspersions on those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another point I strongly disagree with the COP is how my evidence was characterised with regard to Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan's representations in antagonistic terms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I shared my view with the COP that in my opinion, loyalty to Ms Khan was an operative consideration on the minds of Ms Loh and Mr Nathan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe many would take a different view that telling untruths in Parliament is serious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such documentary evidence placed before the COP would show that I had good reasons for concluding that loyalty to Ms Khan was a consideration for her closest allies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ms Loh's perspective of the gravity of what Ms Khan did is one of those good reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once again, such evidence does not appear to have been considered by the COP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could it be to strategically drive a wedge and disunite the Workers' Party and show that its leaders recklessly cast aspersions on their own members?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in making the point, the COP Report carefully omits the only character references I made in reference to Ms Loh and Mr Nathan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote, that "they are decent, good people and have done a lot for the party".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This belief rests on an uncorroborated piece of evidence, a WhatsApp text originating from Ms Khan herself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The COP deems the fact of its contemporaneousness to be critical in coming to its conclusion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The COP does not question Ms Khan's credibility even though she was the one who lied in this House, by her own admission, and even though she also lied when she first communicated with me about this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, if contemporaneous evidence is indeed central, one would expect the COP Report to exhibit a fidelity to such evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, at paragraph 93 of the Report, it makes the case that Ms Loh was surprised the DP was set up and that it advances Mr Nathan's view that the DP was self-serving.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, what were Ms Loh's and Mr Nathan's contemporaneous views on the DP when it was set up?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I submitted my WhatsApp texts with both of them to the COP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once again, this evidence is left out from the COP Report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This leaves me to consider Ms Khan's behaviour after her resignation and her motivations for making her uncorroborated claim at the COP that she was told to take her lie to the grave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would offer that the more natural explanation as to why she would do so is that it was in line with human behaviour, logic and common sense, to use the words of the COP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Her post-resignation behaviour was natural in the arena of political participation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When our first Prime Minister executed the transfer of power from the 1G to 2G leadership, according to five-time PAP MP for Whampoa, Dr Augustine Tan, there was a lot of strain, tension and resentment when older Members and Ministers were told to step aside for the 2G PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In response, one outgoing Minister even spoke against the candidature of Prime Minister Lee at the 1984 elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The comparison with Ms Khan's behaviour and testimony at the COP is apt because not everyone reacts with loyalty to their party or their party leaders when they realise that the curtain is coming down on them or their political careers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How did Toh Chin Chye, former Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the PAP, react when he was pushed to the backbench?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He became a vocal critic of PAP policies and famously said, "How can I remain a dumb cow?" As to the handover of power, he said, "For old party members who had been loyal, it was a painful process.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: You don't repay their loyalty by throwing them out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We had the responsibility to help them find jobs." In fact, so serious was the concern of the unhappiness amongst some members of the PAP old guard about political renewal that the then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew, as Secretary-General of the PAP, suggested to his Assistant Secretary-General Goh Chok Tong to pack new cadre members into the People's Action Party, in case the question of succession and renewal came to the fore at the next PAP party conference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When your departure is precipitated by an overwhelming loss of support from your party members and colleagues, except for your closest allies, from a human behaviour standpoint, I can understand why a person would turn against one's party leaders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My final point, Mr Speaker, is on the legitimate questions raised by Singaporeans about candidate selection in the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As this House knows, and as the Government has also previously shared, for example, when the chief of the Singapore Civil Defence Force was convicted in Court, no selection process is fool-proof, and people can change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even PAP MPs have been found guilty of criminal conduct or forced by their party to vacate their seats for other reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Potential PAP general election candidates have also been substituted at the eleventh hour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The point is that even people who exhibit politically attractive character traits can turn out to be unsuitable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party also has had its fair share of the same experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It can be very difficult, if not impossible, to test a person's judgement in all circumstances prior to fielding them as political candidates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is so even for the PAP, with its massive resources and far greater ease in finding willing candidates, compared to opposition parties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the Workers' Party does not use these realities as an excuse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would include the absolutely legitimate demands of Singaporeans that the Workers' Party field individuals who do not lower the esteem of Parliament, or who do not meet the standards expected of Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, I will object to the Second Motion as the basis for the recommendations is that offences may have been committed by us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of this, I have kept my comments on the COP Report for today's purposes very narrow and limited.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The reality is that in examining the evidence provided by him and his Workers' Party colleagues, MPs, cadre members, and the back and forth, the Committee came to conclusions on the basis of questions that they had, gaps in the logic, and omissions in the submissions of the documents.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The questions, gaps and omissions that he began his statement with are still present, and they are questions, gaps and omissions about what happened within the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What was the truth of the matter between him, his colleagues and Ms Raeesah Khan?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He talks about political partisanship and, unfortunately, the proceedings of the Committee of Privileges would lead a reasonable reader to come to the conclusion that it is him and his colleagues who engaged in political partisanship, by choosing to obfuscate the matter and to deal with Ms Raeesah Khan the way that they did.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He asked why was the Committee of Privileges not interested in getting to the bottom of why Ms Raeesah Khan lied.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He and his colleagues doubt that explanation and he has tried to justify why; I understand.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He asserts his innocence, but he has not yet filled in the gaps and omissions, nor has he answered the questions.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These questions on the facts do go to the very heart of the matter as to whether or not Mr Singh has been honest in his dealings, including with Ms Khan.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And on their own evidence, not a word was spoken about how and when Ms Khan would tell the truth.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In fact, Mr Faisal Manap said zero discussions were had; no question, no comment, despite an extensive discussion about a completely separate matter.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh has not explained how this is possible or even half credible.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why is it that they were able to discuss the clarificatory statement on FGC and polygamy, but felt unable to make a single comment on a far bigger issue, a lie told in Parliament?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Is this credible that this could have happened?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As to their concern about her mental state, why was there not a single word spoken between them, not a single contemporaneous exchange of email messages?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What did they decide to do or not to do?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More importantly, why was there not a single step taken to prepare Ms Khan to tell the truth?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Neither Mr Faisal Manap nor Ms Lim asked Mr Singh what he was doing to ensure that the truth will come out.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Did Mr Singh check with Ms Khan or her parents as to whether they had become aware of the sexual assault?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As Mr Singh has explained, he has perhaps given a bit too much time, but he stated it as a precondition, his foremost concern, he did not once ask about this.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Workers' Party CEC was also not aware, neither were the Party members or cadres.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In short, not a single step taken all the way from August until 3 October, remotely could be construed as preparing Ms Raeesah Khan to come clean and tell the truth.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is an omission, a gap, a question.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But looking at all the rest of the statements, the evidence that is produced, is it not consistent with Ms Khan's account, which is that, if the matter did not come up, she would not have to tell the truth?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh should explain clearly why no steps were taken, if indeed it was important and it remains important for Workers' Party MPs to come clean, to tell the truth, to clarify an untruth told in Parliament, as he claims.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On 3 October, Mr Singh went to see Ms Khan, did not tell Mr Faisal or Ms Lim about this meeting.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He says that he made it clear that Ms Khan should tell the truth.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But he also admits, at the same time, that he did not say to her that she should tell the truth.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Five words. "Raeesah, tell the truth, please." Five words.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why did he instead, say another five words, "I will not judge you"?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Not judging someone is only relevant if Ms Khan was to continue the lie.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There was nothing to judge if she was going to be truthful.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But Mr Singh's conduct tells us something as well.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If he had been clear with Ms Khan to clarify the lie, why did he not respond to Ms Khan on that day and say, "It has already been made clear.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are no two ways about it." Why not insist that she stand up, correct the untruth that she had just repeated?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why not do this when she had just repeated the lie in front of him and the entire Parliament?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And later, when they met, what did Ms Khan say?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh himself said that the first words to him were, "Perhaps, there is another way, that is, to tell the truth".

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Which to a reasonable person, sounds very clear.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Khan was suggesting to Mr Singh a different path away from telling a lie.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Workers' Party stands for honesty, integrity, accountability.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Where was all of that when Mr Singh was privy to a lie being told again in Parliament?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And for all the excuses given about making sure that her father was aware, did Mr Singh ask Ms Khan whether her father was aware already?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It was so important, it was the only reason he offers for Ms Khan not having to come clean earlier.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Yet, at the critical moment, he does not bother to ask, he does not get the details.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Both came away with the clear consensus that he had given Ms Khan an option, a choice.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Completely contrary to what Mr Singh had said to the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is further supported by Ms Lim's own contemporaneous written notes on 29 November Disciplinary Panel meeting with Ms Khan.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh accepts that she, Ms Lim, was accurate in her recording.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh was recounting his own conversation with Ms Khan on 3 October and said, "It was your call".

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Again, an omission, a question left unanswered which runs up against Mr Singh's self-professed understanding that Ms Khan was left with no doubt on 3 October that she would have to come and tell the truth the next day.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On 7 October, the Police sent an email to ask Ms Khan for an interview.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Khan ignored it after counselling with Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why not advise her to come clean if that was so important to them?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If it had been the intention all along for Ms Khan to come clean, explain herself, clarify the lie, then why not cooperate with the Police when they asked?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What is there to hide if you are interested in integrity, honesty and accountability?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Further, Ms Khan then writes to Mr Singh and the others and says, "Thank you for guiding me through this without judgment".

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And according to the various testimonies, as of 7 October, exactly what guidance had been given?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The only guidance that we are clear on her testimony was for her to continue with the narrative and not judge her.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: She had repeated the lie three days earlier.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is the first time that this was expressed: for Ms Khan to tell the truth here in this House, to Parliament.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At no time prior to this did Mr Singh tell Ms Khan that she should tell the truth, including when he had heard her double down on the lie on 4 October.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He first said that Ms Khan was to come clean and raise it on her own accord, regardless of whether it was brought up or not.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If that is the case, then he must have known on 3 October that it will come up one way or another on 4 October.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Which means some preparation would have to be done prior to 4 October.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But when it was pointed out to him that not a single step in preparation was done, he then changed his evidence.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He then said she would bring it up and clarify only if she was asked.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is still a gap, an omission and a question.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And Mr Singh has not provided an answer to it.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But the reality is that none of these questions, which go to the heart of the issue, has been addressed.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are important because they tell us whether Mr Singh has been honest or not in his evidence to the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These also tell us the kind of conduct that Mr Singh is prepared to engage in, in order to keep a lie hidden.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh should come out clearly and tell Parliament what is his response to the specific findings in the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What is his explanation for the various inconsistencies that have occurred on the facts based on his own accord?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What is his explanation for the complete and deafening silence about an absence of steps whatsoever that could have been seen as consistent with wanting the lie to be clarified?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For months, why is there nothing between him, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why is there no contemporaneous communication between them?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Between me and my colleagues, just to settle what time we should meet in order to go through our Parliamentary Questions, we would exchange various pages of emails.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But this, for a most important matter, nothing.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If it is so, it is hard to believe.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What about the Disciplinary Panel, which was set up to look into Ms Khan's conduct?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Why not disclose to the Workers' Party CEC, their own members and their own cadres, that, in fact, Ms Khan had already admitted, come clean to three of the senior Workers' Party leaders, that they had discussed it with her, given her guidance and also disclosed that Mr Singh met with Ms Khan on 3 October?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If indeed he had told her to tell the truth, would that not be relevant to the proceedings of the Disciplinary Panel?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Would that, not mean that Ms Khan had gone against and disobeyed Mr Singh's advice and instructions?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If you look at it as a reasonable person, one conclusion is that Mr Singh's account of the facts did not happen.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Which is why Mr Singh was eager to suppress this highly relevant and critical bit of information – the involvement of all three Disciplinary Panel members and their knowledge from August about the lie.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Still, a gap, an omission and a question unexplained.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Not explaining questions, not answering questions were something that Mr Faisal Manap also did.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He refused to answer questions put to him by the Select Committee.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I was quite struck by how extraordinary this behaviour was when I was watching it.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Watching the video, reading the transcripts, the conclusion I came to at the time is that he knew that saying anything at all would be damaging to Mr Singh and Ms Lim.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But he chose to remain silent, understanding the consequences, because lying under oath or affirmation, lying to a Select Committee, is a serious matter, needs to be dealt with properly.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: People I have spoken to about the Committee of Privileges, my residents, have not always followed the intricate details of the allegations in the testimony.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But when I asked them the question, did Mr Pritam Singh lie, the response is usually one of: "maybe", "possibly", "probably" or "I don't know".

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ordinarily, because that is the standard of the law that should apply to all of us.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh and the Members of the WP have made many speeches – rhetorical flourishes about accountability and transparency.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They put across the idea that these are high principles that they believe in.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But a key test of one's principles is whether you apply them to yourself for a greater good because action speaks volumes, much more than high-soaring rhetoric.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And there is no sign of that action in the details that the Committee of Privileges has recorded about what happened within the WP, away from the public spotlight, their communications, the conduct of the Disciplinary Panel, the statements by Mr Singh, their actions and their inactions.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What now is the right thing to do, given that the Committee of Privileges has found Mr Singh to have lied?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What now is the right thing to do if you are not convinced by the Committee of Privileges Report, but you accept that Mr Singh may have lied?

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This sorry saga has already eroded trust in our institution.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Second, we must consider the impact on the future of our parliamentary democracy.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We would not accept such behaviour among our own MPs or anyone else.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We did not let the matter rest when there was suspicion that Ms Khan lied to the House.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We must hold Mr Singh to the same standard.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In future, there will be mistakes, there will be transgressions.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We must be able to deal with them and MPs must not think they can get away with lying, deceiving Parliament and the public.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They must come clean, apologise and face the consequences.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As a House, we must maintain our standards and our moral imperative to do the right thing now and for the future.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will, indeed, impact upon our democracy and the strengthening of our institutions, but in the opposite way that many members in the media have described.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To oppose the Motions before us is to say that one values who a person is more than what they do – the very opposite of our ideals of meritocracy.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To oppose the Motions is to say that a politically useful outcome is more important than upholding values, to accept the weakening of norms as an acceptable price to pay for political success.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To support the Motions is to fight for a Singapore that is special, where politicians can be trusted and are expected to be honest, capable and upright.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To support the Motions is to fight for a Singapore where politicians do the right thing, not the politically convenient thing.

speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To support the Motions is to believe in our values and our integrity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Perhaps I can ask the Leader of the Opposition where in the Report he sees us use that term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is in my folder; I will reply to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will try and get the information as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think, generally speaking, the nature of the way my decision to bring up Ms Khan's condition was expressed in my speech for three reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is incontrovertible that the COP used very uncharitable, I would even say unparliamentary, words to describe what I did.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, my speech sought to explain why I felt I was legitimate in raising the matter of Ms Khan's condition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And this was the word that occurred to me as to what the COP was trying to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But as the Leader of the House told us just now, the broader issue before us is how democracy should work in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What are the institutions, the norms, the values, that are essential for our democratic system to function properly?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How do we apply these general principles to specific cases, like the one before us now, so as to protect these institutions, norms and values?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And how can we secure our democracy for the future, so that it can long deliver happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are the three more fundamental questions that I wish to discuss today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The quality of a country's democracy hinges on its people's values: what they judge to be right or wrong, what they deem important, the causes they espouse, the ideals they embrace.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whichever example you look at, at whatever point in history, you will find that good and functioning democracies have clear, strong norms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These norms are upheld both by the governed and those who govern them, or those who aspire to govern them one day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is how healthy democratic systems can elect good, incorruptible people with the right values and drive a virtuous cycle where good democracy begets good governance, and good governance begets good politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This cycle must be underpinned and sustained by strong institutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To fulfil its vital role, Parliament must be respected and its Members, processes and proceedings must be trusted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Clear norms and incorruptible values are essential to protecting the dignity and standing of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The system cannot work if the standing of Parliament is called into question.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is why we need to set the right norms of conduct among Parliamentarians and guard them carefully.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If something goes wrong, or something wrong has been done, own up and take responsibility.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do not hide, dodge or spin further lies, to obfuscate and cover up the original fib.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The right norms can only be upheld by people with the right values because norms are not merely social conventions that people comply with for appearance's sake.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to be expressions of internal values that people believe in and hold dear.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is why when taking office, MPs swear "to bear true faith and allegiance to the Republic of Singapore".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, this applies to everyone engaged in Singapore politics, MP or not.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Workers' Party cadre Ms Loh Pei Ying, who was Mr Pritam Singh's former assistant, told the Committee: "It pains me greatly, but to me, beyond anything else, it's important to be truthful to my country".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I believe every Member of this House will agree with her.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our democratic system also depends on the people of Singapore: voters endorsing, insisting on and backing the same norms and values, so that they can discern for themselves – as Ms Loh did – when something is wrong and hold accountable those in power, or aspiring to power, when their actions fall short of these high standards.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is how a democracy can function properly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Inculcating voters and their leaders with the right values is the work of decades.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It takes unremitting effort and passion, and it does not always succeed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most countries are founded and start off on the basis of high ideals and noble values.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But more often than not, beyond the founding leaders and the pioneer generation, over decades and generations, gradually things change.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The leaders, who fought for and won independence, are often exceptional individuals of great courage, immense culture and outstanding ability.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They came through the crucible of fire and emerged as leaders of men and nations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are the David Ben-Gurions, the Jawaharlal Nehrus and we have our own, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Imbued with enormous personal prestige, they strive to meet the high expectations of their peoples to build a brave new world and shape a whole new future for their peoples and for their countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But beyond that initial fervour, succeeding generations often find it hard to sustain this momentum and drive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They start out as healthy democracies with idealism and zeal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But over time, the tone of the society changes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All too easily – a slip here, a blind eye there, a fudge, a trim – and gradually things go downhill.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After a while, the electorate comes to think this is the norm and you cannot expect better.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so, standards get debased, trust is eroded and the country declines further.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many political systems today would be quite unrecognisable to their founding leaders.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Meanwhile, a stream of senior politicians and officials in Israel face a litany of criminal charges, some have gone to jail.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: While Nehru's India has become one where, according to media reports, almost half the MPs in the Lok Sabha have criminal charges pending against them, including charges of rape and murder, though it is also said that many of these allegations are politically-motivated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What is to prevent Singapore from going down the same road?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are not intrinsically smarter or more virtuous than other countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Modern Singapore does not come born with a fail-safe mechanism.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our founding fathers did their best to build strong foundations and institutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even after the Barisan Socialis, which was then the main opposition party, decided to vacate its seats in Parliament in 1966 and left the field entirely to the PAP, our founding fathers maintained our parliamentary democracy and multi-party system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the founding fathers took the more robust way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They kept politics contestable, they built up institutions, Parliament, the Judiciary, the Civil Service, the Police and Armed Forces and, later, the Elected President and the Council of Presidential Advisers to enable Singapore to operate on a more resilient basis, not dependent on a few key people pulling all the levers, pushing all the buttons, making everything work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Still, to operate these institutions, you need good people and they needed to recruit, train and deploy Ministers, Members of Parliament, Judges, civil servants, experts in many fields, people of ability and commitment with a sense of public service and, above all, with honesty and integrity whom Singaporeans could rely upon to do their duty, put Singapore first and make this country succeed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is how the system we have today came to be.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is incumbent on all of us, each succeeding generation, to protect and build upon this system that we have inherited and this requires us to uphold integrity, enforce rules and standards, apply the same rules equally to everyone, make sure nobody is above the law.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we can do that consistently, persistently, unflinchingly, then we have a shot at making things work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: People can trust our leaders, systems and institutions, our democracy can mature, deepen and grow more resilient.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As both the governed and the governing embrace and express the right norms and values, Singapore can continue to flourish.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if we allow ourselves to slacken, loosen standards here just a bit, overlook a lie there just this time, the virtuous cycle will stutter and start to fail.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What is the key factor that keeps this virtuous cycle going, keeps Singapore on the up and not on the down?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On his 100th birthday, Mr George Shultz, the former US Secretary of State, reflected on this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This was a year and a bit ago, December 2020.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He wrote an op-ed upon reaching 100 years old and he said it was one of the most important lessons in his long life that trust is the "coin of the realm". "When trust was in the room," he wrote, "good things happened.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When trust was not in the room, good things did not happen.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Everything else is details." We saw how this worked in the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Trust was a key factor why some countries did better than others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What mattered mostest was: did they trust one another, did they trust their leaders?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore is fortunate to be one of these "high trust" societies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have tried to build upon it during the pandemic but it is something that we have today because we have nurtured it for decades and built it up patiently, assiduously, step by step, never allowing it to be eroded and, therefore, having this with us when we go into battle.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The opposite happened in other countries, for example, in the US and the UK.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the US, trust in the political system has all but broken down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Three-quarters of Republican voters have been made to believe that the last presidential election in 2020 was stolen, that Mr Biden is not a legitimate president and Mr Trump should be the president today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How do you uphold a system when a large segment of the population is convinced that the elected government is illegitimate?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every issue is politicised, government becomes gridlocked, the country suffers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is a key reason why many Americans refused to be vaccinated or to wear masks, why they revolt against measures to keep themselves safe and why they have suffered so many COVID-19 deaths.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or look at the ongoing uproar in Britain about the "partygate" scandal in Westminster, the Mother of Parliaments no less.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The scandal has been attributed to failures of leadership and judgement in an official government report.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore may be a "high trust" society today, but nothing guarantees that we will always remain one.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is essential that we steadfastly maintain our high standards, ensure that we have leaders who embody the right values, call out wrongs when wrongs are done, mete out punishment when punishment is due, preserve the sanctity of our institutions, never take public trust for granted and never allow lies, half-truths and falsehoods to become the accepted norm in politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is what is at stake as we deliberate Parliament's response to the Committee of Privileges' Report.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To deal with this breach of Parliamentary privilege, we convened the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ms Raeesah Khan was called up, as were other witnesses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Committee deliberated extensively before reaching a reasoned conclusion that Ms Khan was guilty and should be fined for each occasion she lied.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hope all Members can agree with these findings and the penalty to be imposed on Ms Khan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in the process of the Committee's deliberations, two other significant issues arose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Committee has drawn them to Parliament's attention and suggested to Parliament how to deal with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If they did, this is surely as serious or more serious than misconduct as Ms Khan speaking an untruth in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Parliament will need to deal with this, but only after we have cleared the second even graver matter and this graver matter is, as the Leader has explained, whether, after having taken solemn oaths to tell the truth, the three Workers' Party leaders told untruths to the Committee of Privileges in order to cover up their instructions to Ms Khan to continue lying.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It became clear to the COP that there were striking contradictions between what the three Members of Parliament claimed to the Committee were their honourable intentions and the hard evidence of what they actually did or very often failed to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And there were serious inconsistencies even between the accounts of the Workers' Party leaders.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Being untruthful under oath is no small matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It means lying despite solemnly affirming that you will tell the truth, in this case, not once, not twice, but repeatedly, over many hours of extensive questioning and on several days.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One, whether the three Members of Parliament instructed Ms Khan to lie; and, two, whether the three Members of Parliament themselves lied under oath.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Both, if established, reflect very badly on the Workers' Party leaders and, in particular, on the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Both issues, if not dealt with properly, will dishonour Parliament and bring this august institution into disrepute.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some asked: was Ms Khan not the one who lied?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Why are the Workers' Party leaders being treated more harshly?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the Leader of the House noted just now, if the Committee is right, then Mr Singh and his fellow Workers' Party leaders themselves lied and presented untruths to the Committee.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They lied under oath to protect themselves, to cover up their role and to push the blame solely onto Ms Khan, claiming that she and other witnesses, like Ms Loh Pei Ying, had lied to the Committee.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is, indeed, more serious than what Ms Khan did, if it is so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By lying under oath, they sought to frustrate the Committee process.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They displayed the same kind of misconduct that the Committee was set up to address.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They betrayed the trust reposed in them as Members of Parliament and, not least, Mr Pritam Singh, the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And this, I hope, Members appreciate, if true, is a very grave matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, Members must decide what Parliament will now do about this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or if that is too much to stomach, given the strong evidence laid out by the Committee, perhaps we lower our standards just a little, note that untruths were told but argue that it was, after all, not so serious a lie and no harm was done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we do either of these things, we, too, would become complicit in dishonouring and demeaning Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must take the transgressions seriously and act on it and I am glad that is the conclusion the Committee has come to and recommended to the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It could have recommended to Parliament to administer a token slap on the wrist.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But that would show that we were taking a very serious matter rather lightly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Worse, by lowering our norms, we would be telling Singaporeans that it is really not so bad for elected leaders to lie.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Alternatively, the Committee could have recommended that Parliament itself metes out an appropriately heavy penalty.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is something that Parliament has the power to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But had the Committee recommended that and Parliament decided on the penalty itself, the Opposition would surely have cried foul and accused the PAP of using its majority to persecute the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I commend this course of action to the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if I were Mr Singh, I would vote in favour of both Motions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Fine Ms Khan, because she is guilty beyond doubt.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, Mr Singh's own party member Mr Dennis Tan, who was on the Committee, thinks she should be fined more heavily for the second offence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if Mr Singh maintains that he and his fellow Workers' Party leaders have done nothing wrong, he should also vote in favour of referring his own case and that of Mr Faisal Manap to the PP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Indeed, he should demand a Court trial, in order to have the full opportunity to defend himself, to vindicate his reputation and clear his name.
