speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is what I would do if I were Mr Singh.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Regrettably, pro-Workers' Party voices on the social media have taken quite a different tack.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Before the matter can be conclusively determined, if necessary, in Court, they are doing their best to confuse the issues and rouse sympathy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are asking the public to clear the names of the three MPs, suggesting that referring the case to the PP is political persecution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What they are really saying is this: do not look too carefully at what Mr Singh did.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is the Opposition that you voted for.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By virtue of his position, he should not be referred to the PP and any action against him must, by definition, be politically-motivated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because who he is is more important than what he has done – even if he may have committed a crime.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some people may be taken in and sympathise with this story.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They say, why not just let the matter rest?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After all, it would be easier for the Government not to have to pursue this matter against the three MPs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But, Mr Speaker, as long as the PAP is the Government, we will not shy away from doing whatever is necessary to uphold the right norms in this House and to imbue Singaporeans and their leaders with the values critical to sustain trust in the system and critical to our success.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Singh succeeded Mr Low Thia Khiang as Secretary General of the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Low served for a very long time – 30 years as an MP, 17 years as party leader.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He sat opposite me, where Mr Singh now sits.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Low was a formidable political opponent, but he was a patriotic Singaporean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He set a different tone for the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said he hoped the Workers' Party could help to build a "First World Parliament" in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He must be saddened that, instead, this is what his successor has done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because what has happened is a betrayal of what Workers' Party claimed that it stood for.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But judging by Mr Low Thia Khiang's public comments, he is confident the party can ride this out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it need not be a setback for our democracy either, provided we hold Mr Singh and his colleagues accountable for dishonouring the standards of this House, and also for possibly breaking the law.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I know Singaporeans want to see more political contestation and I accept that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I expect that is the way Singapore will go in the longer term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is how every parliamentary democracy evolves and it was precisely because I recognised this, that on election night in 2020, after the Workers' Party won a second GRC in Sengkang, I offered to make Mr Singh the Leader of the Opposition and equip him with the resources and support to play this role.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is the way a responsible government can help a credible, responsible opposition to emerge and contribute to the maturing of our political system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the office of Leader of the Opposition carries certain responsibilities: setting the tone for opposition MPs; enforcing standards of conduct on his own party; and, above all, maintaining his own integrity and keeping himself beyond reproach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Leader of the Opposition does not have a blank cheque.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The stakes of today's debate might have been lower if the opposition were a negligible presence, as they were from 1966 until the 1980s.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The public, generally, had low expectations of opposition parties and politicians.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The tone of the country and its governance was set by the PAP and the high standards that the PAP imposed on itself.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But with Singapore heading towards a more contested political landscape, the competence and honesty of the opposition is no longer an inconsequential matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The question of "what are the right values and how should we uphold them?" becomes of fundamental importance for both the opposition and the governing party.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every election, henceforth, will be about who wins the mandate to run this country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the system is working properly, the governing party will be re-elected so long as it remains honest, competent and trusted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the governing party falls short and Singaporeans come to deem an opposition party more honest and incorruptible, more competent and more trustworthy, then the governing party should be voted out, and that opposition party should be voted in to form the next government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We cannot assume that the PAP will always continue in Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Nor can we assume that the Workers' Party, or some other opposition party, or any other opposition party, will always stay in the opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not know when, or how, there will be a change of governing party in Singapore one day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because a small island city-state like Singapore – the only one in the world like this – needs a strong, effective and good government, whoever leads it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr John Major, the former British Prime Minister recently made a speech, triggered by "partygate", I am sure, lamenting the state of British politics today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a cri de coeur cry from the heart.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are told that politicians are 'all the same' and this untruth conditions electors to condone lies as though they were the accepted currency of public life." "But politicians are not 'all the same'.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And lies are just not acceptable." "To imply otherwise is to cheapen public life and slander the vast majority of elected politicians who do not knowingly mislead." "But some do – and their behaviour is corrosive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This tarnishes both politics and the reputation of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a dangerous trend.” "If lies become commonplace, truth ceases to exist.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And where are we then?" "If trust in the word of our leaders in Parliament is lost – then trust in government will be lost too." John Major's is a Western view, but in Eastern societies, too, norms and values are crucial.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, even more than in Western philosophy because Western philosophy says "checks and balances" but Eastern philosophy says "your virtue, your moral standing, that is what gives you the right to govern." In Confucian thought, there are four social guidelines, there is "四维", that hold a state together: rituals, righteousness, probity and shame – "礼义廉耻".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Probity, or desisting from corruption, is about upright behaviour; it is a norm that can be enforced using laws.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But shame, a reaction to wrongdoing, is a moral disposition; it is about one's own sense of right and wrong, whether we know we have done the right thing, or we know we have fallen short even when nobody said so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That has to come from within ourselves, from our own values, our own consciences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Absent that sense of shame, people may comply with laws for fear of punishment, but they will lack the moral compass to do the right thing simply because it is the right thing to do and to take responsibility when they have fallen short of the standards expected of them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The public will mistrust not only individual leaders, or particular political parties, but the whole political system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How can democracy function when there is no one we can trust to put in charge?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How do you put Humpty Dumpty together again?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A democracy not founded on integrity stands on shaky ground and will sooner or later totter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If instead of trust being “the coin of the realm”, as George Shultz puts it, lies become “the accepted currency of public life”, as John Major said, all the sound and fury of contestation and debate will signify nothing good for the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Singapore politics grows more competitive, we must make sure that the competition is honest, impartial and above-board, where the system runs properly and our institutions remain sacred and respected by all, where good people work together constructively to serve Singaporeans, wherever they stand on the political spectrum.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And most basic of all, where Singaporeans can trust those who represent them to conduct themselves honestly and honourably, and act on behalf of the public and of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have scrutinised Ms Raeesah Khan’s actions, and their rights and wrongs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: She has admitted her wrongdoings and will be punished appropriately for them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you tell lies, how can the public trust you?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If someone in a position of responsibility tells lies and visibly gets away with it, how can the public trust the system?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If Parliament condones lying among its own Members, how can Singaporeans trust the institution of Parliament?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we let flagrant, egregious transgressions pass, it will erode trust in our leaders, respect for Parliament and support for our whole political system, and Singapore will be heading for trouble.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the longest serving Member of this House, I feel a greater responsibility for this than most.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When I first entered this House 37 years ago, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Mr S Rajaratnam, Dr Toh Chin Chye, Mr Ong Pang Boon, Mr E W Barker and Mr Jek Yeun Thong were still Members.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Six of the 10 who signed the Separation Agreement on 9 August 1965.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have witnessed first-hand how the founding generation built up this place and handed it to us in good shape.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it should be a sacred trust to every MP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must all never fail to serve Singaporeans to the best of our ability, responsibly and honestly, and uphold this institution of Parliament as the foundation of a robust and healthy democracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I call on all Members in this House, old and new, Government and Opposition, elected and nominated, to weigh the facts, vote with your conscience and join me to do your duty to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the Prime Minister in the main with regard to the sort of political system we want in our country: values of trust, honesty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not disagree with the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second point is with regard to his request to the House to vote in favour of both Motions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We disagree with that because that is basically saying that we admit that we have told a lie to the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And for the same reason, we have to disagree with the Second Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as I made it clear in my speech, I am prepared to clear my name.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And as a result, I will not be objecting to this House resolving to refer this matter to the Public Prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have made the point that I will strive to clear my name not once, but I believe twice: first was in the introduction of my speech; and secondly, in the conclusion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this is what I said, "Should Parliament resolve to adopt the Motion, I intend to clear my name and will fully cooperate with the Public Prosecutor."

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And the Leader of the House mentioned that after the Prime Minister's speech, he would let us know where he saw in the Report the reference to that specific term "weaponised".

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I asked because it is a very specific word, it is a very specific way of characterisation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And this is important for the integrity of the COP process.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, that phrase was debated in Committee and we decided to remove it.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, Mr Pritam Singh would not have reference to the specific term unless somehow earlier drafts were shared with him.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, can he confirm or deny that people told him about the drafts?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Just to confirm before this House, Mr Singh was not referring to any drafts or reference to earlier drafts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There was voluminous material submitted to the Committee and transcripts running to the thousands of pages, which we took time and care to go through.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He, in particular, said that the report did not reflect or did not capture or did not include or did not annex Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhisthra Nathan's contemporaneous views about the formation of the DP as one example of his sense that the COP was not complete in its findings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Singh had cited a few lines from what Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhisthra Nathan had sent in via WhatsApp.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And Members had heard the exchange earlier, their responses to him when he messaged them about the DP hearing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: What Mr Singh omitted to mention were two points.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I would like to read to Members because the Report annexes all of these.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On 10 November, I quote, Pei Ying tells Mr Singh: "Hi Pritam, I've tried to reserve my comment on the Disciplinary Panel so far, but I just saw the message that was sent out to everyone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I feel that it's plain as day to me and people involved in her apology that this is a little backwards paddling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clearly, the party didn't anticipate the backlash despite warnings, and it's trying to do something to quell people's anger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While I agree with it, I can empathise with it, I don't think it is at all fair to let party members think they have a say in this process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If this is done as a mock consultation exercise, then party members will be unhappy their opinions weren't really considered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If it is not a mock exercise, then they will likely ask Raeesah to resign when they do not have the full facts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I welcome the DP to be transparent and share the involvement in this, their findings barring personal information, so the party can make an accurate decision." Mr Pritam Singh replies: "And I hear you, PY, but I do think we need to give party members a platform to have their say on this important matter rather than commiserate privately or between each other and believe that the party leadership decides things without considering their views." Pei Ying replies: "I get that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But the DP hasn't exactly told the party of its knowledge and involvement." Mr Pritam Singh replies: "Despite that it will be good to hear people out." Pei Ying replies: "But their opinions are not accurate because they don't have the facts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Everyone is of the view that we can cut her loose and distance the party from her mistake.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But if she's out of the party, she still subjected to the Committee of Privileges and there's not much we can do to what she says and shares when it gets there." So, that is one set of WhatsApp messages that adds more complexion to what Mr Singh had read out earlier and which was also raised to Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If Mr Singh may remember, at paragraphs 10813, 10814, as well as 10815, 10816, 10817, where that extract was read out to him and he gave his views.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, it is a lot of these materials that are annexed in the Report.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will read it out to Members, in case you have not read it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is very small, but it says at the bottom, in relation to their discussion with Mr Singh, immediately, they contemporaneously exchanged messages with each other.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And Ms Loh Pei Ying said, "Pritam just told me himself about the disciplinary committee… he didn’t say much more".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yudhisthra Nathan said, "He sent me the same message too".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Loh Pei Ying replied, "I wonder why he is informing the both of us tho… I asked him if we would be questioned… he said no".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yudhisthra Nathan said, "OMG lol, tht didn’t cross my mind… I think he wanted to tell us just so we heard it from him before the party pg which is nice I guess...

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I do feel he n Sylvia underestimated the backlash”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Loh Pei Ying said, “funny he made the special effort to tell the both of us but not rae?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also think he’s being too reactionary… I would have let it simmer for another 2 days", so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the bottom, Ms Loh Pei Yong said: "Here it comes”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yudhisthra Nathan said, “he also being dragged”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Loh Pei Ying said, “so i don’t trust Pritam to put himself above things lol… like when it affects him personally, I’m worried he’ll cut the cord”.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Speaker, it still does not answer the point that I brought up in my speech about the contemporaneous evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The fact of the matter is, the COP relies on contemporaneous evidence and puts a high probative value on it in certain cases, but Mr Desmond Lee just read out a narration of text messages between Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan, which is on the record, and my point is, I have submitted documents to the COP, which are not on the record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the Committee was minded to send us a summons to produce, we produced documents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have also raised other examples in my speech, I am not going in my speech, I did not go into it, to the detail that I would have wanted because there is a recommendation to refer the matter to the PP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We are always told that it is important, when a matter is under investigation, let us not comment too much.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I should be given that right as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But Prime Minister has gone one step further and said: "Go to trial!" I mean, that is certainly Prime Minister's view.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But my point still comes back to the point I made in my speech and I do not believe Mr Desmond Lee's clarification deals with it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I would request is for the Committee to return all those documents to me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I made a request to Speaker on Friday that all that evidence which I have submitted, including the cover letter, is returned to me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe I mentioned cover letter, but I mentioned documents and the cover letter is part of it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I hope this will be done, because that is not in the Committee of Privileges' Report.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will just say in response to that, Mr Speaker, that the Committee did not rely purely on contemporaneous messages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It looked at the whole suite of action or inaction, that is quite plain from the Report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Speaker, can I confirm whether those documents will be returned to me?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Committee will respond to you formally on that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 6.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.50 pm until 6.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Janet Ang, perhaps you might like to deliver your speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, would Mr Faisal Manap be speaking?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, Mr Speaker, but I think he is doing his prayers now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Sylvia Lim is not in the Chamber either.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It must have been a very painful and difficult journey for all involved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have listened to as many of the key recordings and read as many of the key transcripts as I could, and I am satisfied with the process and the effort that was put in by the Committee to establish the truth of the situation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, I did not binge-watch; I actually watched one at a time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Honesty, integrity and trust are the badges of honour which have put Singapore on the world map.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That is how we have earned the reputation of high trust in business, diplomacy, Government and society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We hold one another to high standards and, almost always, we are not prepared to bend the rules or close a blind eye.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is not easy to hold up to high standards, but that we must.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As individuals, every day, we have the freedom to discern and choose to do what is right and shun the temptation to take the easier road which could be to choose to do nothing, to do the popular thing, or to do what will result in less criticism and less trouble for ourselves.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is a daily test in every encounter with every situation and person I meet to make the choice to do the right thing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But, of course, we are human and, despite our best efforts, we are not saints.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We do make wrong judgements and, sometimes, there may be good reasons that led us to that bad call.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding, a bad call is a bad call and we have to deal with it – own up to it, seek forgiveness and make amends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With respect to the COP findings, I thought long and hard if there are other options that the COP could have taken.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister has earlier on also alluded to – if you and I were in the COP, what would we, or could we, have recommended differently?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Trust is difficult to earn but easily broken.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, to do the right thing takes courage, but I hope we can also do the right thing with compassion.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Speaker, I support the recommendations, and the Motion as set out by the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These notes were used as evidence against Mr Pritam Singh to support the finding that he had given Ms Raeesah Khan a free choice to continue the lie she had told in August.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is necessary for me to correct misconceptions that have arisen from the COP's findings here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The COP further notes, among other things, the following: Paragraph 237(3): "Ms Lim, a lawyer and Chair of the Workers' Party, would have appreciated the effect of such evidence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be, and was, extremely damaging to the testimony given by Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It directly contradicted Mr Pritam Singh's evidence that he did not give Ms Khan a choice." Paragraph 237(4): "Ms Lim was clear in her testimony that a choice to tell the truth cannot be given to the Workers' Party Members of Parliament, an obvious point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That was also directly contrary to what Mr Singh had done and Ms Lim recognised that." Speaker, I take a different view.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If read in the proper context, my evidence is not inconsistent and not damaging to Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it is consistent with his evidence that he was telling her she had to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had testified that the extracts from my notes had to be seen in totality to understand it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, let me quote the extract from my handwritten notes which were recorded in the form of question and answer. "Question by PS (Mr Pritam Singh): Before October session, I met you and told you it was your call.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did need to tell the truth in Parl (Parliament) occur to you?" "RK (Raeesah Khan): Yes, but consumed with guilt and own experience.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thought it wouldn't come up." "PS: Can't lie, right?" "RK: Yes." Sir, just looking at this extract, we see that when Mr Pritam Singh said to her: "Can't lie, right?", Ms Khan did not contradict him.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She said: "Yes", which is an acceptance that you cannot lie.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does this not mean that she understood what he meant all along that she had to tell the truth?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When he put to her that she could not lie, she did not say that she was given a choice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I was puzzled as to why the COP stated that, I examined the footnotes used by the COP for this conclusion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I submit that the evidence I gave does not support this finding.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For this, please allow me to refer to the transcripts of evidence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The COP cited footnote 421 as the basis for saying that I was clear in my testimony that a choice to tell the truth cannot be given to Workers' Party MPs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had also stated at the same time that I could not imagine Mr Pritam Singh giving Ms Khan a choice, and I did not believe it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That puts a totally different complexion on the paragraph cited by the COP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Later in my testimony, I was asked by the Chairman about the notes I recorded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was questioned repeatedly about whether I agreed that the phrase "it is your call" could be interpreted as giving her a free choice to decide whether to tell the truth or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The COP finds that I recognised that Mr Pritam Singh had acted contrary to a Member of Parliament's duty to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For this, it quoted my evidence from transcripts at paragraphs 12936 to 12945.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Please let me spend a little time on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here are the paragraphs that the COP relied on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At paragraph 12936, the Chairman said: "In that last page, you mentioned regarding the conversation on 3 October.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the top of the page where Mr Pritam Singh said: “Before the October session, I met you and told you it was your call.” So, meaning that it was really up to her to decide what to do."  And my answer was, "I don’t know the context but he phrased it in this way."  Then the Chairman asked, "From this, it would seem to be that it’s really for her to decide, which is, I guess —", and I said, "She has to decide, yes." And the Chairman said, " —I guess, if you follow from this, when he said that: 'I will not judge you', is that 'You decide what you want to do, I will not judge you for that'.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would that be a fair interpretation, as you see it?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I know you were not there —" And I said, "I wasn't there."  Then the Chairman continued, "I'm saying that as from what he has recounted here, as you have recorded, and what we know now of what would had been said specifically, this would be a reasonable interpretation of it?...

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That line came from Mr Pritam Singh himself who said: ‘to take ownership and responsibility, I will not judge you’."  "So, I’m just asking", that was the Chairman asking me, "based on what Mr Pritam Singh has shared, and given what he said now here, would that be a reasonable interpretation, that it was really left for her to decide?"  And my answer, "Well, I mean, I don't know what he said because I've put myself on a news block-out for the last few days.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But in any case, it is recorded as it is recorded, yes." The COP then cut off its reference abruptly here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, up to this point, I was, at best, telling the COP that I was not there at the meeting on 3 October.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where was there any recognition by me that Mr Pritam Singh had done something contrary to the duty of an MP to tell the truth?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, the COP ignored the next four paragraphs which show that the Chairman was still continuing his clarifications with me, which I shall now read out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Paragraph 12946, "Chairman: Just to remind you, the specific line he said was: 'to take ownership and responsibility and I will not judge you'.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, these few lines came out across clearly as what he conveyed." And I said, "Okay".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And the Chairman said, "And I'm just asking you, that based on what you've recounted here, it would suggest that the option was left to Ms Khan to decide what to do".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And my response was: "I think it also has to be looked at in the whole context, because what we recorded here was that: 'I told you it was your call, did the need to tell the truth in Parliament occur to you?' Then she says: 'Yes, but I was consumed with guilt in my own experience and I thought it wouldn't come up.' Of course, she’s not saying here: 'You gave me a choice, so I made that choice'.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She says: 'I was consumed with guilt in my own experience and I thought it wouldn't come up.' And he says, 'But you can't lie, right?' And she says: 'Yes'.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, it has to be taken, I think, in totality to understand it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Like I said, I wasn't there but this is what I recorded." So, Mr Speaker, these last four paragraphs were curiously excluded from the COP's footnote 422, even though it was part and parcel of the Chairman's clarifications on the same topic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If included and properly understood, I submit that my evidence does not support the COP's conclusions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How they approach this matter has serious ramifications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There has been public discussion of the composition of the COP, as it is overwhelmingly dominated by ruling party Members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I find the state of affairs unsatisfactory as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As it currently stands, the Committee only has one out of its eight Members from the opposition Workers’ Party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This does not bode well for a fair hearing in Parliament, where the ruling party has a super majority of 90%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is public interest to ensure that elected MPs are subject to fair parliamentary hearings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One way towards this is to have a more balanced composition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My suggestion is that Parliament consider amending the Standing Orders on the composition of the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is likely to result in a less one-sided hearing and fuller consideration of relevant evidence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to some observations of the COP process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, on representation before the COP, I would like to ask how the Committee decided on conducting the questioning of witnesses by itself?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a past COP in 1986, Parliament resolved to have questioning conducted by a law officer of the Legal Service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further resolved then that lawyers be allowed to represent the MP and other persons as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems to me that such a process is better.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would enable the Committee to sit back and concentrate on evaluating the evidence dispassionately, rather than have Committee Members actively positing a certain case theory and trying to break witnesses down.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If legal representation is allowed, there may be less need for Parliament to make referrals of cases to the PP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Members of the public have noted the strenuous questioning of Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mr Faisal Manap was questioned for about six hours in a single day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Mr Singh’s case, the questioning was done for nine hours in a single day, which, including waiting time, took 12 hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While my own questioning was less than three hours, I waited for two days in a guarded room and was denied the use of any communication devices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I needed to visit the bathroom, I was accompanied by security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I requested to use the disabled toilet to have more space, permission was sought.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our Courts of law do not subject witnesses to such treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also commented briefly on the referral to the PP that Parliament will be voting on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And I have also made my own observations about COP processes and why I think reform is needed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I had given evidence to the Committee of Privileges on 9 December last year in a session that was nearly six hours long, as mentioned by Ms Sylvia Lim just now.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, I will not touch on and repeat what I presented at that session.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because I am sure that at the end of this debate, this Motion will be passed, and Mr Pritam Singh and I will be referred to the Public Prosecutor for further investigation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will give my best cooperation to the investigation that will be carried out.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, it is more appropriate for me to give a statement later at the appropriate time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Meet-The-People sessions, weekly house-to-house visits and other efforts will continue as usual.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Concerns were also relayed about my situation and Mr Pritam Singh’s situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Besides concern and worries, many have expressed support, words of reassurance and confidence, and quite a number of people also wished us well and sent prayers our way.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In facing this current situation, we are confident that we will continue to survive, persevere and carry on with our mission to contribute to the formation of a democratic society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sad because one of the Members of Parliament (MPs) has admitted to lying before this House and the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sad because this whole incident has been protracted as the allegation and lies were left uncorrected for many months before the truth was finally revealed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I regret the manner in which the young activists who boldly came forward to give evidence at the COP proceedings have now been alleged by their own party leader that they may have lied out of loyalty to the former Member, disregarding the many years of service and activism.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, this is not the way young people, who only came forward to serve the nation, not just the party, should be treated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I regret the manner in which the former MP has been characterised both by her own party's leadership and some members of the public, the same ones who had lifted her and backed her to the hilt before aspersions were cast about her mental health and the nature of the trauma that she suffered.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not the way that survivors of sexual violence and people suffering from mental health issues should be treated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In discussing this incident, whether during the COP proceedings, this Motion or elsewhere, let us all have some regard and consideration for common decency.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us all also have regard to the feelings of survivors of sexual violence, people who suffer from mental health issues and young people who are watching us today.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Our responsibility to the people and in protecting the trust in the democracy of Singapore is a heavy one and should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Trust is earned when our actions are equal to our words and we walk the talk.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But once that trust is lost, things will never be the same again.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The actions of the former Member were clearly wrong.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She has admitted her wrongdoing and we are now debating the issue of an appropriate punishment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But she is a young woman with no experience in politics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to her, her party leaders told her to keep to the lie but they turned on her and, subsequently, she had to resign.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To have a first-class democracy, we need good contestable politics, in the best interest of the people.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In ensuring that, we need to attract young people who will place Singapore and Singaporeans first; before party or politics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order to attract and retain young people to be involved in shaping the politics and future of Singapore, we need to have party leaders on both sides of the aisle who exemplify high moral courage and characters of great integrity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Not leaders who are the first to turn their backs on the young or leave them in the lurch in their time of need.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The meetings, according to him, lasted two to three hours on each day.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He was asked about the documents that Mr Singh and Ms Lim brought to the meetings but he refused to answer the question.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even though he was asked about the materials which Mr Singh and Ms Lim brought to the meetings, he still refused to answer the question.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Or anyone else among us could have done?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ms Raeesah Khan looked up to and got advice from Mr Faisal Manap as a senior Malay/Muslim Member of Parliament in her party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He is the Vice-Chairman of the party and someone who has had many years of experience as a politician.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She asked him to guide her and give advice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And this was evident in the communication messages between them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to Ms Khan, she was advised to take the lie to the grave, and when exposed, she was eventually sacrificed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the critical time during the COP proceedings, Mr Faisal Manap chose to remain silent rather than answer the question posed by the COP.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where is the compassion for a young person in need?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does this show exemplary and honourable character and morals?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As minority MPs who are Muslims, we also reflect the values, morals and principles of our community and faith, as responsible leaders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As they say in the olden days: "Leaders must be capable Earning the trust Displaying bravery Bound to promises and vows Given the responsibility For leaders are chosen by the people Revered by the community Placed high on a pedestal And status accorded appropriately" (In English): We need to earn the right to lead and the respect to be called leaders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With sadness and regret, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards the first Motion, the conclusions of the COP and the recommendations flowing from these conclusions are obvious as Ms Raeesah Khan had admitted to making the untruth.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will elaborate on my support of the second Motion, that is, the Motion to refer the conduct of Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Faisal Manap to the PP.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The facts underlying the second Motion arose in the course of the COP’s inquiry into the untruth.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In order for the COP to have come to its conclusions, it must have inadvertently formed its mind on the testimony given by the persons who had appeared before it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As set out by the COP, and as mentioned by the hon Leader of the House earlier, Parliament is perfectly equipped and empowered by law to deal with these two matters itself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, the conclusions and recommendations of a fresh set of COP procedures considering these two matters are highly unlikely to depart from the conclusions already reached in the present proceedings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the potential punishment that may flow from a finding of guilt may have political consequences, in particular, affecting the make-up of Parliament and would, inevitably, suffer from the mien of being politically motivated.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This was also mentioned by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The gravity of the offences, if made out, would then be lost in such circumstance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, Sir, I would be extremely uncomfortable if the COP’s recommendations were the opposite, that is, for Parliament itself to take action against Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap based on the facts that arose from the COP's inquiry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If the matter goes to Court, Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap would also be able to avail themselves of the adversarial process in criminal proceedings, with all the protections of the Criminal Procedure Code and the application of the higher evidentiary threshold of beyond reasonable doubt for criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I am glad that Mr Singh has said that he intends to cooperate fully with the PP, and the points that he and Mr Faisal Manap and, in fact, that Ms Lim made earlier as well are relevant and can be raised in these proceedings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This should be a position that sits well with all parties in this House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Both the Government and the Opposition have expressed in this House and recognised that the Courts should be the impartial arbiters of truth in matters where there may be political consequences or overtones.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, this was precisely one of the positions taken by the Workers’ Party as regards FICA last year.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Courts are also alive to this role as an independent arbiter in matters that may have a political hue.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In a decision in 2020, in which the Court of Appeal considered a matter where the convicted party sought to vary his sentence from a fine of $5,000 to a jail term so that he would not be disqualified from running in the next elections, the Court of Appeal held: “…it would bring the Judiciary and the administration of justice into disrepute if we were to impose sentences with an eye towards the political process.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: After all, a Court that chooses to impose an inappropriate sentence in order to avoid disqualifying a candidate from standing for election as a Member of Parliament could just as easily do the same thing to achieve the opposite end.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In truth, both outcomes are equally abhorrent and impermissible”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Court of Appeal added that: “the only guide for a sentencing Court is that it must strive to impose a condign sentence”. "Condign", of course, meaning "appropriate".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think, Sir, that it is a foregone conclusion.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There had been instances in which the Courts have decided against the Government, even in favour of an opposition political party.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Members may recall that in an October 2021 decision, the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal, in part, by the Singapore Democratic Party challenging a Correction Direction by MOM.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In its grounds of decision, the Court of Appeal set out its reasons in extent as to why it allowed the appeal.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We can expect that the Court will undertake a similarly rigorous examination of the facts and the law in these matters, as it does on all matters.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that Mr Singh had also said earlier that he expected that he would get a fair hearing if it went to that.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I trust that all parties will allow the legal process to run its course, from the PP’s consideration of whether an offence is disclosed, to, if it turns out as such, the deliberation and ultimate decision by the Court.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Parties, whether represented in this House or otherwise, should not cast aspersions on the Office of the Public Prosecutor and on the Courts, especially if the ultimate outcome is not one they expected or had hoped for.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While this matter involves members of political parties, Sir, I do not see the recommendations as political machinations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But equally, where there is no wrongdoing, an accused person must have a fair chance to vindicate himself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Not only must it be a fair chance, but it must also be seen to be a fair chance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Politics is politics, Sir, but the facts are the facts, and the law is the law.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, thank you for letting me join this debate.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The saga involving former Member of Parliament Ms Raeesah Khan's lies has now culminated in the Report of the Committee of Privileges, published on 10 February.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I read it with a very heavy heart.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The core issue of the Report is about lies.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms Raeesah Khan first spoke an untruth in Parliament last August, which is already no small matter.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) leadership was found to have guided her and condoned her in perpetuating the lie.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even worse, WP leadership was found to have lied to the COP in attempting to cover up their role in the saga.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is a major problem which needs to be dealt with seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But some question whether things are truly this serious.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some WP sympathisers pointed out that the majority of COP members are from the PAP and painted the proceedings as bullying.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even some among the ruling party's own supporters are worried that it will be penalised by the public opinion.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clearly, the Workers’ Party is prepared to make the most of such sentiments, as evidenced by its statement issued on 11 February, suggesting that if Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Faisal Manap are referred to the PP, then the work of the COP is politically-motivated.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These sentiments have obscured the central point, that is, as a democratic country, can we tolerate lying politicians?

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Every voter votes for the party he supports, and governments are formed from the outcome of popular elections.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Voters must be able to trust that political parties and candidates are truthful and do not spout untruth at will.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Only then can electoral outcomes reflect the will of the citizenry.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If politicians are free to lie and act in a way that is inconsistent with their words, then voters cannot trust political parties.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Elections become meaningless and our democratic system would gradually disintegrate.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Of course, we cannot count on every politician being irreproachable in his conduct and values.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There should also be safeguards built into the system.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is why contempt of Parliament or lying in Parliament would be subject to investigations by the COP, and penalties meted out by Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Lying to the COP would be dealt with more seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If there are still questions regarding whether the person giving evidence is truthful, then our Courts would be the final arbiter of the truth.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Any democratic society that hopes for stable governance must commit to upholding the truth.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The problem is that the truth is never universally popular.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A responsible ruling party will not lie, nor should it.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But this also creates space for its opponents to use half-truths or empty promises to win support.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When faced with an honest ruling party with a proven track record, every opposition party can choose between two paths.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The first path is to deal only with the truth, point out where the incumbent has genuinely fallen short in terms of its policies and propose workable alternatives.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The second path is to opportunistically and cynically distort the truth and inflame emotions, all for the sake of winning more support and votes at little cost.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A responsible opposition party should commit only to the first path and stoically reject the second path.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In a democracy, dealing only with truths that are not universally popular comes with a price, which is why both incumbent parties and opposition parties face an ever-present temptation to relax their commitment to the truth.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is a temptation that is as dangerous as the temptation to be corrupt.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As the people's representatives, we have to stay vigilant about the thin end of the wedge and guard against lies, however small, while party leaders must hold themselves and their Members of Parliament to the highest standards.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: All parties must fully support mechanisms that protect the truth.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: What weighed on me is that the COP Report shows that the Workers' Party leadership is leaning not towards the first path, but towards the second path.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They have demonstrated an opportunistic and cavalier attitude towards the truth, when it came to deciding whether Ms Raeesah Khan should own up, and when and how it should be done.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, when they came to know about Ms Khan's lie, the Workers' Party leaders did not cause her to clarify immediately and proactively.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They tried their luck with a "wait and see" approach.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If the matter was not brought up, Ms Khan was to "take the information to the grave".

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clear conflicts of interest were present in the hastily convened Disciplinary Panel that was announced by the Workers' Party on 2 November.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: All the blame for doubling down on the lie was pushed onto Ms Khan.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The CEC subsequently resolved that she should resign or be expelled from the party.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The COP was tasked to investigate this case.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But when the Workers' Party leaders appeared before the COP, their performance was even more chilling.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When asked about the impact of Ms Khan's lie on the reputation of the Police, Mr Pritam Singh attempted to minimise the issue.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: His view was that the Police was not a "broken-back" organisation, implying that it was, therefore, alright to make false allegations about them.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He also claimed that he had not required Ms Khan to clarify the truth as he wanted her to have time to inform her parents of her sexual assault.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But as he did not follow up to see if this was indeed done, this excuse proved incredible.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Workers' Party leaders also suggested that Ms Khan might be mentally affected and possibly more prone to lying due to her having been a victim of sexual assault.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This was proven to be baseless by a mental health professional.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She lost her party membership as well as her parliamentary seat.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I imagine that over the past few months, every day would have been unbearable for her.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If she had heard what Mr Singh said about her earlier, she would have been cast under an even darker shadow.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that she can walk out of that shadow and soldier on bravely and optimistically.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, the Workers' Party as a whole, and its supporters.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: You only need to read the statements by party cadres Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudishthra Nathan to feel their pain.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The scant regard for Parliament's dignity and credibility demonstrated by Workers' Party leaders, despite being Members of Parliament themselves, has undermined its prestige.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The statements made by Workers' Party leaders have reinforced the prejudices that these people already face.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Condoning the lies and being cavalier with the truth already undermine the foundation of honesty and trust that our democracy is built on.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But if party leaders, including the Leader of the Opposition, lie, then it must be looked into seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The behaviour of a party leader sets the tone for the values of the entire party and is critical to the preservation of healthy dynamics within our political ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It snowballed beyond control because those involved kept trying to cover their tracks.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Nonetheless, before the debate today started, I had held out hope that the Workers' Party leaders could be forthright and sincere and support the two Motions.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, the speeches of the three Workers' Party leaders earlier showed no intention to make things right.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They seem to have made up their mind to carry on with perverse prevarication.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If so, our democratic system would simply have to deal with their tactics every step of the way.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that when all is said and done, the Workers' Party leaders can come to realise the meaning of the idiom “a country is nothing without the people’s trust”.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For other Workers' Party Members of Parliament, it is not too late yet.

speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope they can support the two Motions based on their conscience and their initial resolve to serve the people, so that the Workers’ Party can shake off the shadow of prevarication, choose to be truthful and get back on the right track.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will now call upon Leader to make a reply on both Motions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have raised a number of points, but the points do not really address the core of this matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not address the key findings of the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I can understand, tactically and strategically, why you do that, because you have got this big uncomfortable report that says these really strong statements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is probably, as a strategy, a good idea not to deal with those head-on, but to pick small little things here and there, and to hope that other people will look at that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But since that is how it has been presented to this House, let me address all those small little points first, before I come back to the key issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first thing Mr Singh had said is that it has been something like 25 years since we have had to have proceedings before the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it is a very shameful thing that we had to have a Committee of Privileges for something like this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For so many years, we were able to do without it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But now, after we have the office of the Leader of Opposition, we have Workers' Party coming in, and then, we have to deal with this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I suppose when these things happen, they serve as a good reminder to all of us about the values that we uphold and the things that we need to do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in some ways, this process has been educational.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first part, we know, was off her own bat.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That was something she did of her own accord.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She admits it; it is not in dispute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The big question was why it was done on 4 October.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And reams and reams of paper have been directed at precisely that question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I do not think one can say that the Committee of Privileges did not want to get to the bottom of why she lied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The next thing Mr Singh said was the fact that she had concocted the lie was not balanced against her evidence to the COP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The allegation is that she has lied before, she must be lying again.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Courts which deal with this, it is known as the similar fact evidence rule.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Just because somebody has done something once, does not necessarily mean that they are guilty of the same thing again.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you want to get to the bottom of something, if you want to get to the truth of something, you always have to look at each instance by itself and weigh it objectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is exactly what the Committee of Privileges did.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I do not think that that is a fair accusation to level against the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The next thing he mentioned was the selective nature of the COP Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It did not mention certain documents, he said.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But then, as we can see, when he made reference to certain WhatsApp messages, Minister Desmond Lee read out other WhatsApp messages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I mean, there was so much evidence, you cannot possibly be referring to every single piece.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But what is clear is that the Committee took into account and considered all relevant documents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the essence of the allegation by Mr Singh is that the Committee had cherry-picked the evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He knows that evidence that is given is considered by a tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Not all evidence that is put in is relevant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And when you write your final report, you refer to relevant evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If he feels that something is relevant and was not taken into account, he will have the opportunity to refer to it, if this matter goes to Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But then, what is important is that, at this point of time, we should not try to give the impression that the COP purposely left out certain things or cherry-picked evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I come now to Ms Lim's speech just now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think she made reference to the notes that she took during the Disciplinary Panel proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And obviously, because that piece of paper, those notes were very damaging to Mr Singh, she sought to explain it, to put her interpretation on it and to suggest that this was not really taken into account by the COP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think at paragraph 51 of the Report, the Report expressly quoted her as saying that her notes had to be taken in totality to understand it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It said that Ms Lim said she did not know the context in which Mr Singh used the phrase and essentially the Committee noted her position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is not as though the Committee did not consider the things that Ms Lim said just now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other thing is Ms Lim said much about the fact that the notes did not just refer to the words "It was your call".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The notes also had the phrase "Did the need to tell the truth occur to you", "can't lie, right?" And she suggested that those notes were really in favour of Mr Singh.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That was dealt with at paragraph 55 of the Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The way the Committee dealt with it was, they said that those questions were quite telling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Mr Singh had been very clear on 3 October, then Mr Singh would be saying, "I told you to tell the truth and you did not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You went against my instructions in telling the truth to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That was a serious breach of party discipline." He would not be saying as he did, "I have told you that it was your call.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Why it did not occur to you to tell the truth" and "can't lie, right?" So, in short, the points that Ms Lim talked about just now were something that the Committee considered, and it is in the Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, the next strategy is really to cast some aspersions on the COP itself and to suggest that, somehow, there is something wrong with the composition of the COP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, what the Standing Orders seek to do, is to make sure that the Select Committee, which is a standing Select Committee, reflects the same balance that is here in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And Mr Singh has spoken many times about why do we not have more Select Committees, and about the supremacy of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, all of these are in the rules which have been there for a long time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And these rules, they have been revised from time to time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if I recall correctly, I believe Mr Low Thia Khiang was on the Committee for the revision of the rules at one stage.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And nobody has complained about the composition of the Committee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, in fact, when we had to determine who would be the Opposition representative on the Committee of Privileges, Mr Dennis Tan was nominated by Mr Singh and he certainly did not complain at that time, or say that he should have more Opposition Members.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it just really rather does sound as though, if you do not like the outcome of the Committee of Privileges, then you complain about how it is composed, when it was never an issue before.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, I think Ms Lim talked about the length of the proceedings, why was it necessary to question Mr Singh for so long.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is that the length of time that it takes to do an inquiry or to question somebody, really depends on the answers that they give.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The witnesses who give you the answers in a straightforward and straight manner, actually go off very quickly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The ones who do not give a straight answer, the ones who you really have to extract the information from, those take a long time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, Ms Lim’s evidence was relatively short, because the answers that she gave were to the point.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, I should also say that she questioned how come there was no legal representation on the Committee of Privileges for the people who appeared before it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, the default position is that, for the Committee of Privileges, generally speaking, they do the questioning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But by special application, where it is necessary, if there is good reason for it, witnesses can apply to bring outside counsel.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I think the more important point to remember here is that Mr Singh is a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not think they really needed external counsel to be able to answer the questions that were put to them, which were not particularly difficult – well within their ability to understand and respond to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, now, I come to the point about what these speeches did not address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You would think that from the time that it is disclosed to them, the first reaction should be: "Oh, no, this is terrible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But no, this matter dragged on for one month, two months, three months.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it only came about after the Police had already put in their request for an interview and it became clear that this issue was not going to go away.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other is this very puzzling thing about why there was no direct instruction to tell the truth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I mean, how difficult is it to just say, "Raeesah, tell the truth"?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Anybody should know how you can do that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this business of asking Ms Khan, being worried about her telling her parents, or have the parents found out, if that was so, how come nobody asked her whether she had told her parents?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Why was no effort made to find out if she had cleared that, so that she could come back to Parliament and tell the truth?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And why was their own party not told about it?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How do you have a Disciplinary Panel that is set up to sit in judgement upon somebody, to judge her for something where, in fact, she has already told you – you know what she has done from months back?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But you are sitting there, in judgement on her.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as I wrap, let me just wrap where Mr Singh began when he said, "Who did this House commit to the Committee of Privileges – Raeesah Khan or the WP leadership?" Now, that is somewhat misleading.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You see, under the Standing Orders and the way the procedure goes, when a complaint arises and it comes to Parliament's attention, Parliament has to deal with it somehow.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in this case, once Ms Khan came to Parliament and admitted that she had lied, it had to be looked into.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I referred it to the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Committee of Privileges was inquiring into the complaint about her.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But in the course of that, these things came up and it became clear to the Committee of Privileges that there is a problem.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because they think that the three senior WP leaders were lying and had guided her to not tell the truth in Parliament, until there was no other choice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What is the Committee of Privileges supposed to do?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It was not set up to look into the three WP leaders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if you are then seized with information, or it comes to your attention, that the three WP leaders have done something wrong, the Committee of Privileges has a duty to come back to Parliament and tell us, which they have done in the Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we here, in this Chamber, now have a duty to consider it and to do something about it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are only three things we can do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One, we can just say, "I am not going to look at it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not want to deal with it." And that would be wrong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be wrong for all the reasons that the Prime Minister has said.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be wrong because it would be an abdication of our responsibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it would be wrong because it is a rejection of our values.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second thing we can do is to say, "Okay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us punish them straightaway." But then, Mr Singh is saying that he denies this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He is saying that they did not do these things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And so, you could ride roughshod, you could steam roll, but that is not the right thing to do either.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because just like Ms Raeesah Khan was inquired into, somebody has to inquire into this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is, you set up another Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the COP has said they do not think it is going to get very far because they have pretty much heard what there is to hear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, whatever it is, we cannot run away from the fact that we have before us a Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will be entitled to legal counsel, legal representation and it will go before the Courts who are independent and they need not fear that there is any political interference.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think, Mr Speaker, I have dealt with the various things that have been raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
